description: Salutations, stranger! This is Steve's Stellar Space Software Syndicate. We supply superb space software solutions to support seemingly all your spacefaring needs!
summary:
Surprisingly Simple Space Surveying System turns real space data into an interactive discovery game. Built for curious students, casual explorers, and amateur astronomers, it brings NASA’s SPHEREx infrared imagery and WISE/NEOWISE observations into an accessible sky viewer. Players explore the sky, compare observations across time, inspect spectral information, and check sources against astronomical catalogues such as ESA’s Gaia and SIMBAD.

Inspired by One in a Krillion, our leaderboard makes exploration rewarding and encourages players to return, investigate, and share interesting findings. The goal is to turn curiosity into evidence-based learning: a surprising object becomes a reason to ask questions, compare data, and understand what astronomers observe.

Our project addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by making infrared exploration approachable while preserving scientific context. Observations, predicted positions, and possible candidates remain clearly distinguished; an unusual finding is an invitation to investigate, not a confirmed discovery. By combining gamification, multi-mission data, and accessible visualization, we help more people participate in the process of exploring our universe.
details:
From curiosity to investigation

Surprisingly Simple Space Surveying System turns astronomical exploration into a game built around real observations. Our starting point was the excitement of finding something rare in One in a Krillion. We adapted that inspiration into a leaderboard and an exploration loop: explore the sky, notice something interesting, compare the evidence, and record a finding.

We designed the experience for curious students, casual players, and amateur astronomers. A player does not need to begin with expertise in infrared astronomy. An unusual point of light provides a reason to investigate, while deeper catalogue and spectral information gives experienced users more to explore.

What the project does

Our browser-based sky viewer lets users navigate to a position or named target, inspect SPHEREx infrared imagery, and explore wavelength layers. Where suitable observations are available, users can compare dated images with blink and time-lapse controls. WISE/NEOWISE provides a separate historical comparison workflow. Source inspection connects the visual experience to catalogue information, and findings and leaderboard interfaces make investigation feel purposeful.

The central interaction is simple: choose a target, compare what is visible, check what is already known, and decide whether an observation deserves further attention. We treat a candidate as a question to investigate, not as a confirmed discovery.

NASA data is the foundation

SPHEREx spectral images and its all-sky mosaic, served through NASA/IPAC IRSA, provide the core infrared experience. We distinguish wavelength layers in a mosaic from observations taken on different dates: moving through wavelengths is not the same as watching an object move through time.

The WISE workflow uses original WISE/NEOWISE single-exposure images, with unWISE metadata helping locate exposures. ESA Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD provide complementary source context. The project also includes catalogue-review integrations for CatWISE2020, UltracoolSheet, SkyBoT, and VizieR, plus a manually requested NEOSSat image-reference lookup. Archive availability and coverage vary; an unavailable check is different from a search that returned no matches.

How we built it

The interface uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and the Aladin Lite sky viewer. Python services handle archive access, astronomical image processing, and catalogue queries. The project includes findings and leaderboard components and a Supabase integration for shared persistence. Our demonstrated configuration uses local-browser findings and leaderboard storage; a shared production deployment still requires configuration.

For image comparisons, the processing workflow places compatible observations on a common sky grid and applies a shared display stretch. Retained real examples support repeatable demonstrations. Observation dates and source provenance help users understand what they are looking at, while synthetic development fixtures remain separate from real observations.

Creativity and intended impact

Our contribution is the combination of gamification, multi-mission context, and an evidence-first exploration workflow. The leaderboard provides a reason to return; the scientific context provides a reason to think. We aim to lower the barrier between looking at a space image and asking an informed question about it.

This could support classroom inquiry, independent learning, and public engagement with astronomical archives. These are intended benefits, not measured adoption or learning outcomes. Our prototype demonstrates the experience; broader impact will depend on user testing, reliable hosting, and further refinement.

Scientific care and next steps

We considered archive outages, incomplete coverage, image artefacts, saturation, and the risk of mistaking visual differences for discoveries. Catalogue measurements, predicted positions, and image observations are distinct. Blink comparisons are quick-look tools, not validated measurements of motion or variability. Next steps include stronger candidate review, accessibility testing, more robust shared deployment, and evaluation with learners and astronomy enthusiasts.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

We used SI throughout planning, research support, coding, debugging, testing, documentation, visual layout, and presentation preparation. SI helped us develop and communicate the project; the astronomical observations come from the credited scientific archives. Our demonstration uses actual program captures and original vector graphics, with no generated sky imagery. The repository SI_USE.md document describes our workflow and credits the One in a Krillion inspiration.
